reviewed.by: ROUND 4 — argument x2, citations x1, orthodoxy x2. Orthodoxy re-gate returned CLEAN (0 heresy / 0 drift / 0 note) on round 3; argument re-gate returned 1 BREAK + 4 WEAK, all fixed here. STANDING CONSTRAINTS, do not undo: (1) The CLOSE must not argue about date or authorship. The original close, 'details no forger would think to invent', was an authorship claim that contradicted the scope bound 12 seconds earlier, and it is invalid against the actual critical position -- a LATE AUTHOR WITH ACCESS TO BABYLONIAN MEMORY is not an inventor. Daniel's date divides orthodox Christians, so a date claim forfeits denominational neutrality. The close is now the essay's own final sentence. (2) THE HEDGE MUST GOVERN 'that is because'. Montgomery (ICC) reads taltiy as an OFFICE title (Akkadian shalshu, 'thirdling'/triumvir), on which the first-two-places-taken arithmetic dissolves entirely. What the Aramaic controls is the INFERENCE, not the cuneiform fact -- Nabonidus and Belshazzar holding the top two places is not in doubt. Round 1 moved the hedge onto the inference and hardened it to 'the natural reading'; round 3 dropped 'that is because' from the CARD, which hedged the uncontested fact and left the contested inference bare. Both are the same defect. (3) THE CARDS AND THE VOICEOVER ARE TWO SEPARATELY SHIPPED SURFACES AND THE CARDS ARE THE MUTED PATH -- which is the majority path for a reel. Every compression the cards made in rounds 1-3 dropped a hedge or a bound (scene 5's attribution, scene 6's 'from the events', scene 12's 'that is because', scene 14's 'or the events', scene 16's 'case after case'). CHECK BOTH SURFACES ON EVERY EDIT. (4) 'An earlier generation of critics' and 'one of the telltale blunders' -- the essay's own words. No serious critic has used Belshazzar against Daniel since Dougherty 1929, and Belshazzar was never the linchpin; the modern late-date case rests on the Greek loanwords, the Aramaic dialect, placement in the Ketuvim, and Daniel 11, and Darius the Mede is the problem specialists call hardest. Undated 'critics' or 'the giveaway' misrepresents an abandoned position as a live one. (5) Keep 'on its own' in the scope bound (leaves the cumulative case open) AND keep BOTH halves -- the date bound and 'or confirm the events it narrates'. The second half is the essay's signature setting-not-truth rule and the card had dropped it. (6) Never say archaeology 'proves the Bible', and never say no find has ever contradicted a biblical claim (retired 2026-07-28; NOTE: that claim has NO entry in tools/retired-claims.json, so nothing catches it mechanically -- add one). (7) Do not claim critics doubted Pontius Pilate's existence; he is attested by Tacitus, Josephus and Philo. (8) 'but the crown was still his father's' -- 'still' resolves it against scene 8's 'entrusted the kingship' as power delegated, title retained, which is footnote 8. Do NOT revert to 'he was not the king': that contradicts scene 2 and hands over the standard 'Daniel calls him king and he wasn't' objection. (9) Scene 14 = man-and-authority bound; scene 15 = archaeology-does-not-prove; scene 16 = close. Scenes 12, 14 and 15 are the guardrail scenes: if the voiceover must be trimmed to fit, take the words from scenes 1-8, NEVER from these three.

voiceover: For a long time, one name in the Bible had no evidence outside it. Daniel five tells of a feast in Babylon, a hand writing on the wall, and a king named Belshazzar. No Babylonian or Greek source knew him. The king lists ended the dynasty with Nabonidus. In the records anyone had read, there was no Belshazzar. So an earlier generation of critics concluded: the author of Daniel did not know Babylon. On their reading, he had got Babylon's kings wrong. It was treated as one of the telltale blunders — a mistake showing the book was written late, by someone far from the events. Then the cuneiform was read. A cylinder of Nabonidus names his eldest son. Bel-shar-usur. Belshazzar. And the records say something stranger. For years Nabonidus was not even in Babylon. He was at Tema, in Arabia, and he entrusted the kingship to his son. So Belshazzar was real, and he was ruling — but the crown was still his father's. He was second, and he stayed second. Now go back to Daniel five. Belshazzar offers a reward to anyone who can read the writing, and what he offers is oddly specific. Not second. Third. On the likely sense of the Aramaic, that is because the first two places were already taken — by Nabonidus, and by Belshazzar himself. An odd detail turns out to fit a political arrangement lost until the cuneiform was recovered. Be careful here. It establishes the man and his authority. It does not, on its own, settle when Daniel was written, or confirm the events it narrates. Archaeology does not prove the Bible, and anyone who tells you it does is overselling. What it does is this: case after case, it shows the writers knew their world. And a source that reliable deserves to be weighed, not waved away.
